list.listitem: Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) is potentially lethal and requires rapid recognition and treatment to prevent death. Suspect it in patients with abdominal pain that is out of proportion to the examination, especially with a history of cardiovascular disease. C
Mesenteric arteriography is the gold standard for diagnosing obstructive and nonobstructive AMI and chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI). C

AMI treatment often includes laparotomy with surgical revascularization and necrotic bowel resection, typically with second-look surgery 24 to 48 hours later. Treatment can also include endovascular therapy to repair an obstruction, or aggressive resuscitation if AMI is due to a nonobstructive cause. C
Intra-arterial papaverine or prostaglandin E1 is associated with improved outcomes in patients with non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia in the ICU. B
CMI treatment can include surgical or percutaneous endovascular revascularization. B

background.definition: Acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) is a sudden obstructive or nonobstructive process within the mesenteric blood vessels that causes insufficient perfusion to maintain intestine viability. CMI, or intestinal angina, is the intermittent, transient occurrence of inadequate mesenteric blood flow severe enough to produce symptoms.

list.listitem: A systematic review found that the mean incidence was 6.2 cases per 100,000 person-years of follow-up. They further estimate that 5 of every 10,000 hospital admissions are due to acute mesenteric ischemia.
Early diagnosis is critical to avoid the increasing mortality associated with delays in surgery from symptom onset.
At least two thirds of patients with either AMI or CMI are women.

Nonthrombotic causes (60% of cases): low-flow states (hypovolemia, cardiogenic shock, sepsis), mechanical causes (strangulation, intussusception), trauma, aortic dissection, drug-related causes (vasoconstrictors, cocaine, ergots), post-vascular surgery.
Thrombotic causes (34% of cases): arterial embolism, arterial thrombosis, venous thrombosis.
Nearly always because of atherosclerotic disease of the mesenteric vessels causing partial or complete obstruction.

Ninety-five percent of patients have two of the three mesenteric arteries (celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries) involved, 55% have all three involved, 7% have isolated superior mesenteric artery occlusion, 2% have isolated celiac artery involvement.

AMI is the rapid onset of decreased blood flow to the intestines, due to: partial or complete obstruction of the mesenteric arteries or veins (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric); or nonocclusive processes, most commonly low-flow states, but may also be due to mechanical causes, trauma, medications and drugs, and postvascular surgery.
CMI is caused by repeated bouts of temporarily diminished blood flow through the mesenteric arteries.
It is most commonly caused by stenosis or occlusion by an atherosclerotic plaque.
Symptoms may be exacerbated or triggered by food ingestion and the increased metabolic needs of digestion.
Patients with acute abdominal pain out of proportion to the examination who have a history of cardiovascular disease should be evaluated for AMI. B
Mesenteric arteriography is the gold standard for diagnosis of both obstructive and nonobstructive AMI, as well as CMI. C
Patients with a history of cardiovascular disease who develop postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss without explanation should be evaluated for CMI. B
Duplex ultrasound, CT, and MRA are acceptable initial tests for the diagnosis of CMI. C

Differential.Differential_Features: More commonly associated with diarrhea; possibly fever; typically a short symptomatic course
Typically left lower quadrant abdominal pain with inflamed diverticula on abdominal CT scan
Obvious air-fluid level pattern on abdominal radiograph; history of recent surgery
Presents with fever, ascites, abdominal pain; history of cirrhosis or previous peritonitis common
Periumbilical pain progressing to right lower quadrant (RLQ) pain at McBurney's point; characteristic CT scan findings
Positive Murphy's sign; positive findings on right upper quadrant (RUQ) ultrasound
Pain radiating to the back; history of ulcers, alcohol use, or NSAID use common; confirmed by endoscopy
Epigastric pain radiating to the back; inflamed and edematous pancreas and surrounding tissue on CT

list.listitem: Most patients (>90%) present with sudden onset of abdominal pain, often out of proportion to examination findings.
Postprandial abdominal pain, usually generalized, lasting 1 to 3 hours, and progressively worsening over weeks to months is typical.
Fear of abdominal pain leads to decreased appetite and weight loss.
Vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation are less common symptoms.

Patients may present with a leukocytosis, elevated lactate level, metabolic acidosis, elevated serum phosphate level, and elevated BUN and creatinine levels. No laboratory test, however, is sufficiently sensitive or specific to rule in or rule out AMI or CMI.

A systematic review concluded that interleukin-6 (sensitivity 96%, specificity 83%, LR+ 5.6, LR- 0.05) and procalcitonin (sensitivity 80%, specificity 87%, LR+ 6.2, LR- 0.23) were reasonably accurate for AMI.
In patients with a venous thrombosis as the cause of AMI, a hypercoagulable state work-up should be performed; one third of patients may have a protein C or protein S deficiency.

A systematic review concluded that d-dimer is highly sensitive (93%) so a normal d-dimer makes the diagnosis less likely. Lactate and neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio were highly specific for acute mesentheric ischemia.
Ultrasound, CT angiography, and MRA are reasonable initial tests for the diagnosis of CMI. Early diagnosis is challenging, but CT angiography is the current gold standard.

CT angiography is highly accurate for diagnosing AMI. Findings suggesting mesenteric ischemia include the following situations: (1) if any of the following findings are present: pneumatosis intestinalis, isolated superior mesenteric artery occlusion, celiac and inferior mesenteric artery occlusion with distal superior mesenteric artery disease, arterial embolism, or venous gas; or (2) if there is bowel wall thickening plus one of the following: focal lack of bowel wall enhancement, solid organ infarction, or venous thrombosis. Several meta-analyses confirmed this diagnostic performance, finding it was 92% sensitive and 98.8% specific (LR+ 92, LR- 0.08). The value of this diagnostic test is best optimized when used in conjunction with a thorough clinical examination.

Ultrasound may be used as an initial diagnostic test for chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) in stable patients with chronic kidney disease or a history of severe reactions to iodinated contrast. Ultrasound can detect ostial lesions at the aortic origins of the mesenteric arteries, but its ability to detect lesions distal to this rapidly diminishes. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound using wideband power Doppler techniques is a new technology that shows promise in detecting intestinal ischemia; it may show absent or diminished color signals within the least peristaltic segment of intestine and has a sensitivity of 94.1%, a specificity of 100%, a positive predictive value of 100%, and a negative predictive value of 97.1% for intestinal ischemia.

Peripheral mesenteric artery obstructions are more difficult to identify with ultrasound or contrast-enhanced CT—if clinical suspicion remains high for mesenteric ischemia, a negative ultrasound or CT result should not preclude the decision to perform angiography. US and CT cannot diagnose nonocclusive causes of mesenteric ischemia, such as low-flow states and vasospasm.
Catheter arteriography is the gold standard for the diagnosis of AMI and CMI, and can identify obstructive and nonobstructive causes of mesenteric ischemia.
Arteriography can also allow for catheter-directed therapy, and if surgery is required, can provide information on the location and severity of lesions.

A study of 184 patients (50 with CMI) calculated a mesenteric artery calcium score using computed tomography, and found that using a cutoff of >16 for celiac artery was 85% sensitive but only 53% specific. For SMA, it was 74% sensitive and 62% specific using a cutoff of >29.0. Negative predictive values were 91% and 87% for CA and SMA respectively.
Laparotomy should be emergently used as a diagnostic and therapeutic tool when patients present acutely with severe abdominal pain and peritoneal signs.
The inspection of the bowel by an experienced surgeon remains the most effective and reliable diagnostic tool to identify infarcted bowel.

Patients, especially those with a history of cardiovascular disease, with abdominal pain severe enough to present to a physician that is out of proportion to examination, and whose clinical presentation does not suggest some other etiology, should be evaluated for AMI. See .
CMI should be considered in patients who present with postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss without another explanation, especially those with a history of cardiovascular disease.
In patients with nonocclusive AMI, rapid and aggressive treatment to reverse the underlying low-flow state is the first and most critical step in treatment. C

Laparotomy with surgical revascularization and resection of necrotic bowel is indicated for patients with acute abdominal pain, peritoneal signs, and suspected AMI; a second-look surgery may be indicated 24 to 48 hours later. B

Percutaneous endovascular treatment for AMI is acceptable in selected patients and is associated with lower mortality in observational studies, but laparotomy may still be necessary to evaluate for necrotic bowel.B

Transcatheter administration of vasodilators (papaverine or prostaglandin E1) is indicated in patients with nonobstructive AMI not responding to resuscitative measures or nonobstructive AMI because of cocaine or ergot poisoning.B
Surgical revascularization or percutaneous endovascular treatment are acceptable treatments for CMI. B

In patients with nonocclusive AMI, potentially reversible low-flow states should be rapidly and aggressively treated to correct the underlying cause (sepsis, hypovolemia, cardiogenic shock, and so forth).

Intraarterial papaverine is indicated for use in nonocclusive AMI, and can be used in occlusive AMI when surgery is contraindicated, when there are no peritoneal signs, and perioperatively to inhibit intraoperative and postoperative vasospasm of mesenteric vessels.
Other vasodilators, besides papaverine, used for nonocclusive AMI include prostaglandin E-1 and nitroglycerine.

Successful use of thrombolytic therapy (streptokinase, urokinase, tPA) has been described in case reports; its use is contraindicated in known or suspected bowel infarction, which limits its widespread use.

Cardiogenic arterial emboli (ie, emboli because of atrial fibrillation) and mesenteric venous thromboses that cause AMI should be treated with anticoagulation therapy (heparin or warfarin) for 3 to 6 months.
Perioperative heparinization for arterial emboli from noncardiac sources may be considered.
Currently there is no role for drug therapy in CMI treatment.
Early diagnosis is critical to improve the success rate of surgery and improve survival rate.
Laparotomy is indicated if any peritoneal signs are present.

With laparotomy, the surgeon can perform revascularization surgery by surgical endarterectomy or bypass grafting; identify viable, nonviable, and questionably viable segments of bowel; and resect any infarcted bowel.
A second-look laparotomy 24 to 48 hours later can be considered to reexamine questionably viable segments of bowel.

Endovascular therapy is an alternative option to revascularization surgery, but still often requires a laparotomy for assessment of bowel viability. Endovascular therapy includes percutaneous interventions involving balloon angioplasty, stenting, and transcatheter delivery of a vasodilator (papaverine) or other thrombolytic therapy.

A systematic review identified seven observational studies comparing endovascular with open surgical approaches. Mortality was lower in the endovascular group (15% to 39% versus 33% to 50%) but selection bias and confounding are likely in the absence of randomization. A second systematic review identified 8 observational studies comparing endovascular therapy with open surgery for patients with AMI (n=8185) and reported an odds ratio of 0.45 favoring endovascular therapy (95% CI 0.30-0.67). The same caveats about observational studies apply, though.

A systematic review found 12 studies with 335 patients (all observational) who had non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia. They found lower mortality in those undergoing some sort of local vasodilatory treatment (largely with intra-arterial papaverine or prostaglandin E1) and found an association between treatment and lower mortality (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.10-0.71).

Surgery by endarterectomy or bypass grafting in limited case series has shown high revascularization success rates (98%-100%), 30-day mortality rates of 9% to 11%, and recurrence rates in 1 to 3 years of 19% to 24%.

A systematic review identified 22 observational studies comparing endovascular therapy with open surgery for patients with chronic mesenteric ischemia. Open surgery was associated with a lower 3 year recurrence rate (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.34-0.66) and similar survival but a higher risk of post-procedural complications (RR 2.2, 95% CI 1.8 - 2.6).

A systematic review identified one RCT and 5 observational studies comparing bare-metal with covered stents forf chronic mesenteric ischemia. Covered stents were associated with more favorable outcomes.

A Danish registry study of 245 patients with CMI treated endovascularly foun generally good results, with 85% one year and 74% three year survival. Results were less favorable for patients with acute on chronic mesenteric ischemia (1 and 3 year survival of 67% and 54% respectively). Outcomes were better for superior mesenteric artery involvement than other sites.
Steerable introducer sheaths may be more effective for treatment of celiac or superior mesenteric artery lesions based on limited data from a series of 66 patients.
Long-term follow-up is mandatory for patients treated for CMI.

Long-term care of patients with CMI includes adequate control of the patient's blood pressure, lipids, and blood glucose levels, and lifestyle modifications (ie, a cardiovascular-healthy, low-salt, low-fat diet and regular exercise).
AMI mortality, even with treatment, is approximately 70% and has not changed in several decades; without treatment, it is likely fatal.B
Early diagnosis and treatment are key to improving AMI survival rates. B
CMI survival rates are similar between surgical and endovascular revascularization, but with a lower recurrence rate after surgical repair. B
Untreated CMI will likely lead to AMI or death because of increasing weight loss and malnutrition. C
Asymptomatic mesenteric artery stenoses and obstructions do not require revascularization, but may be considered during aorta or renal artery surgery for other indications. B
Nearly always fatal without treatment: intestinal ischemia leads to infarction, bowel perforation, peritonitis, and ultimately death.
Rare exceptions occur when ischemia is limited to the mucosal layer or when the progression of AMI is slow enough to allow collateral circulation to form and compensate.
In one retrospective analysis, acute mesenteric thrombosis (versus dissection) on CT scan predicted a higher likelihood of adverse outcomes.
A systematic review reported a 60% mortality for patients hospitalized with AMI.

A systematic review of observational studies reported 40% mortality for open surgery, 26% for endovascular therapy, and 32% for retrograde open mesenteric stenting. Selection bias would be an important explanation for some of the differences seen, which have remained stable over time.
Risk factors for mortality include increasing age, chronic renal disease, hypotension, large bowel involvement, and heart failure.
Patients with untreated CMI likely progress to AMI or continue to lose weight until death.
The percentage of patients with CMI who develop AMI is unknown.

Asymptomatic mesenteric artery stenoses and occlusions may be incidental findings during diagnostic procedures for other conditions. There is no evidence that these patients are at increased risk for developing AMI or CMI or have a higher mortality rate than control patients. Surgical revascularization is not indicated for asymptomatic patients, unless undergoing aorta or renal artery surgery for other reasons.
The mortality rate of patients with treated AMI has held at an average of 70% over the past several decades.

Arterial thrombus has the highest mortality rate of all the causes of obstructive AMI; venous thrombosis has the lowest rate. Arterial embolus has a better prognosis than arterial thrombus or non-occlusive ischemia.
Mortality is increased when time from symptom onset to hospital admission is greater than 24 hours, and when there is colonic involvement.
With surgical or endovascular treatment, most patients with CMI have favorable outcomes.

Surgery by endarterectomy or bypass grafting in limited case series has shown high revascularization success rates (98%-100%), 30-day mortality rates of 9% to 11%, and recurrence rates in 1 to 3 years of 19% to 24%.

Endovascular therapy (stenting, angioplasty) is also used, but has less favorable outcomes: revascularization success rates of 80% to 93%, 30-day mortality rates of 11% to 13%, and recurrence rates in 1 to 3 years of 27% to 46% are not as favorable as with surgery.

cell.label: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion with examination with no other explanation, or other evidence suggesting AMI? Stabilize the patient, correct any reversible or contributing causes.
Peritoneal signs?
Laparotomy.
Treat as appropriate.
History of DVTs or hypercoagulable state?
Mesenteric arteriography. May consider CTA, but negative finding does not rule out AMI.
Obstructive AMI?
Mesenteric venous thrombosis or arterial thrombus or embolus?
Peritoneal signs?
No evidence of collaterals or superior mesenteric artery filling is poor or absent?
Continuous papaverine infusion. Percutaneous endovascular therapy (stenting, balloon angioplasty, thrombolytics) may be considered; observation alone is an alternative. Consider repeat angiogram.

Laparotomy. Perform revascularization (embolectomy or bypass grafting). Resect segments of infarcted bowel. Consider papaverine infusion, if possible. May consider thrombolytics as alternative to laparotomy.
Consider repeat angiogram and/or second-look laparotomy in 24-48 hours.
Peritoneal signs?
Anticoagulation for 3-6 months.
Laparotomy, resect segments of infarcted bowel. May consider papaverine infusion, thrombolytic therapy, or thrombectomy.
Anticoagulation (heparin). Consider second-look laparotomy in 24-48 hours.
Anticoagulation (coumadin) for 3-6 months.
Nonobstructive AMI.
Continuous papaverine infusion. Correct underlying cause (hypovolemia, shock, sepsis, congestive heart failure, vasoconstrictors, etc.).
Laparotomy if peritoneal signs or evidence of bowel infarction. Resect segments of infarcted bowel.
Consider repeat angiogram and/or second-look laparotomy in 24-48 hours.
CT with contrast. Mesenteric venous thrombosis present?
Treat as appropriate.
